# Body Spray SDK: AXE and Surface

> The Body Spray SDK lets an agent drive an existing web application through the controls people already use, with the same availability, reasons, and handlers. For ordinary ChatGPT users, the target production path is `plugins/agent-experience` plus the provider-operated `mcp/` service: the person installs one public plugin, and a relevant request selects a trusted connector and starts an identity-isolated hidden application browser whose Surface is used entirely inside the agent conversation. The consuming application runs no MCP server. Install `@summationai/axe-surface` and `@summationai/axe-relay`, run `axe surface init --app-id <id> --app-name <name>`, and mount the generated provider above login and account/workspace resolution. Surface is enabled by default; add a feature flag only deliberately. The generated `<SurfaceProvider>` keeps authoritative live state and a structured application profile in the page, while the hidden service transports generic `relay_*` and `surface_*` tools without a pairing code or visible browser. `@summationai/axe-surface/auto` derives the surface from the page's accessibility semantics, every entry states its guarantee tier (`derived`, `annotated`, or `declared`, in the entry field `tier`), a reviewed `SurfaceConfig` (`rules: [{ match, ... }]`) refines it, and `axe surface coverage` shows what the page could not say and suggests the config. Browser-native WebMCP remains an additional direct path where the host supports it. Deeper tiers stay available: declared registration (`useSurface`, `register`) for exact controls, and server-side AXE actions (`createAXE`, `action()`) served over MCP (`@summationai/axe-mcp`), WebMCP (`@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp`), or HTTP (`axe/0.1`, whose manifest does not by itself make agents discover a site). Every result uses one envelope with five statuses (`ok`, `needs_input`, `needs_human`, `pending`, `error`), approvals bound to the exact call, and retries that replay a completed operation. This file is for an agent about to integrate the SDK into an existing application. Every name below exists in this repository; each link points at the source of the claim.

> Architecture invariant: The provider registry says where an application is and how it may be connected securely. The application's Surface says what the application currently is and what the agent can do there. The MCP contains no application-specific behavior.

AXE is outside-in. A site declares actions with `createAXE` and `action()`, wrapping functions it already has; clients discover `/.well-known/axe.json`, call `POST /axe/actions/{name}`, continue at `/axe/continue`, resume at `/axe/resume`, and read what can be done right now at `/axe/state`; `@summationai/axe-mcp` derives an MCP server from the same manifest. Surface is inside-out. The application registers each control that matters (an `action`, a `field`, or a `collection`) with a stable `id`, a `name` that states the outcome, its `state` with a `reason`, its `effect`, and the very handler the control runs; `observe()` is an indexed snapshot at a revision and `act()` runs one control under a revision guard. Surface has three rules ([spec/SURFACE.md](docs/spec/SURFACE.html) section 2): Surface reports, it never decides ([S-RULE-1]); same door, an act runs the control's own handler ([S-RULE-2]); one revision, every observation carries it and every act presents it ([S-RULE-3]). The seam is `@summationai/axe-surface/axe`: `surfaceActions(surface, { namespace, auth })` is an `ActionProvider` for `axe.addProvider` whose set is `<ns>.observe`, `<ns>.ledger`, and one action per entry, with the entry's live `state` as the action's `availability` and its refusals mapped onto the ladder; `domainActions(surface, { namespace, domains })` serves the same surface as a fixed set of parameterized actions. Every action either bridge generates requires `auth: "user"` unless the integrator writes otherwise. Discovery, MCP, kinds, conformance, and the audit then apply unchanged.

## Add Surface with the company-side MCP service

The default desktop-agent path keeps state and execution inside the consuming page and uses the provider-operated service only as transport. It is `docs/getting-started.md` ("Add Surface to an existing app"), with relay contracts in [spec/SURFACE.md](docs/spec/SURFACE.html) §9, the browser-agent contract in §8, and derivation contracts in §10. The service entry point is `mcp/`; no service dependency is installed in the consuming application.

- Install `@summationai/axe-surface` (entries `.`, `/react`, `/auto`, `/axe`, `/webmcp`) and the browser-only `@summationai/axe-relay/client`. Nothing is on npm yet; install the `core surface relay` tarballs as in "Packaging". Do not install `@summationai/axe-mcp`, the MCP SDK, or `ws` in the application.
- Run `npx @summationai/axe surface init --app-id <id> --app-name <name> --dry-run`. It detects the framework (React Router 7 framework mode, the Next App Router, Vite React, React under another bundler, plain HTML), package manager, and root, then prints one root wrapper plus a generated `surface.tsx` and empty `surface.config` overlay. The generated provider is enabled by default, publishes a structured profile, exposes browser-native WebMCP where available, and accepts an injected provider connection. `--flag`, `--flag <module>#<export>`, or `--flag-hook '<call>' --flag-import <module>` deliberately adds a rollout gate. `--yes` applies it, a second run changes nothing, `--install` runs the package manager, and `--vendor <dir>` installs from tarballs with the matching override. Then `npx @summationai/axe surface prompt > integrate-surface.md` gives a coding agent the judgment part.
- Register the application in the provider's connector registry with its URL, allowed origins, identity mapping, session strategy, and expected Surface id. Run the provider service from `mcp/`, not from the consuming application. Its stable endpoint exposes generic `apps_search`, `app_connect`, `relay_*`, and `surface_*` tools. A single connector is selected automatically; multiple connectors are selected by id after discovery. `--relay-dev` and pairing remain a local attended-tab diagnostic only.
- What easy mode derives ([S-AUTO-2] to [S-AUTO-6]): `SurfaceProvider` (or `useAutoSurface`, or `autoSurface()` outside React) starts in an effect, reads roles, accessible names, disabled states and their descriptions, values, and the dialogs, landmarks, and headings controls sit in, and registers one entry per control on the module-level `surface`, so declared entries share the table. Keys are `<route>#<containers>/<role>:<name>` (numeric and UUID segments become `:id`); pin one that must never move with `data-surface-id` or a rule's `id`. Native links and non-destructive router buttons inside a navigation landmark are low-risk navigation; put `data-surface-navigation` on the exact custom button that only changes location when the DOM otherwise cannot express that intent. A click is the pointer, mouse, and focus sequence plus `click()`; typing uses the native value setter plus `input` and `change`, so React's `onChange` runs. After an act the surface waits for the page to settle, re-scans, and reports `changed` and `notices`. Every observe row that is not declared carries `tier`: `derived` (from the page), `annotated` (refined by a rule or `data-surface-*`), and declared (absent: `register`, `useSurface`, a config `declare`, or a rule's `handler`). A derived act cannot put `expectedRev` into your server's write, because a click has nowhere to carry it; the surface still refuses a stale act within the tab, and a write that must be checked on the server belongs in the declared tier.
- Refine with config ([S-CFG-1] to [S-CFG-8]): a `SurfaceConfig` is a plain object reviewed in a diff: `rules: [{ match: { key, id, selector, route, role, name }, name, object, id, role, reason, state, effect, sensitive, editable, hide, approval, group, handler }]`, plus `app`, `routes`, `lexicon`, `policy` (`allow`, `approve`, `deny` per risk level), `groups`, `sensitive` and `exclude` selectors, `declare`, `landmarks`, and `navigate`. Every matching rule applies in order and later fields win. A rule's `handler` runs the application's own function instead of the page's events, which makes that control declared without touching its component. `checkConfig` returns a config's problems as sentences; `handle.configure(next)` swaps it in and re-scans.
- Measure: `npx @summationai/axe surface coverage <dev-url> [--routes /a,/b] [--auth ...] [--out coverage.md] [--json]` opens the app in headless Chromium through Playwright (installed by the app), calls `window.__surface.coverage()` on each page, and prints one Markdown report: counts by kind, tier, and name confidence, the entries waiting on approval, stale rules (`staleConfig`), and gaps (unnamed and icon-only controls, weak or duplicate names, clickable elements with no role, canvas charts, cross-origin frames, virtualized grids, file inputs, closed shadow roots, unrecognized effects), each with the markup fix and a rule to paste. In the page, `handle.coverage()` and `formatCoverage` give the same. Coverage is not a score; each gap is the next edit.
- In the browser-native path, the agent uses the WebMCP tools registered by the page. `surface_observe` returns the live table and revision; an auto surface also registers `surface_read` for bounded/redacted visible content and `surface_wait` for slow page work; one tool per eligible control calls the page's own `surface.act`. High-risk, explicitly confirmed, and approval-gated acts require `requestApproval`; the application records the person's approve or deny decision and opens the one-use derived approval gate only after approval. Without that trusted callback the call returns `approval_channel_missing` and does not act. The browser host must implement `document.modelContext.registerTool` and deliver those tools to the current task: a generic headless/browser-automation session with only click/type primitives is not a WebMCP host and cannot be repaired by prompting. In development, a provider with `expose` publishes `window.__surface.webMcp()` to distinguish unavailable, registering, ready, degraded, registration error, and closed states.
- In the desktop-agent path, the standalone `mcp/` service exposes `relay_tabs`, `relay_select-tab`, `relay_pair` in development, `relay_stop`, `surface_read`, `surface_observe`, `surface_set-field`, `surface_run-control`, `surface_load-more`, `surface_wait`, and `surface_ledger`; the page remains the state owner and the service transports snapshots, acts, and decisions.
- `RelayConnection.stop()` is an explicit user revocation, never lifecycle cleanup. React effects, route teardown, and other ordinary unmounts call `disconnect()` so the relay keeps the tab available for a remount; the generated integrations already make this distinction.
- [docs/auto-surface.md](docs/auto-surface.html): easy mode: the three tiers, what is derived, safety defaults, configuration, coverage, tools, what is not derived.
- [docs/host.md](docs/host.html): the optional unattended remote adapter: what the application needs, local development (`axe host login`, `axe host --dev`), production (`createHost`, `sessionFor`, OAuth), security, and limits.
- [docs/chatgpt-plugin.md](docs/chatgpt-plugin.html): the consumer phone/desktop path: public plugin, OAuth connection, automatic browser-tab handoff, and the consent boundary.
- [mcp/README.md](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/mcp/README.md): run and configure the standalone company-side service for desktop agents.
- [docs/relay.md](docs/relay.html): the service's browser-to-agent transport: attended and unattended modes, approvals and Stop, tenant switches, production, security, and limits.
- [docs/getting-started.md](docs/getting-started.html): "Add Surface to an existing app", the optional remote path, then "Serve actions over AXE".
- [packages/cli/src/surface/detect.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/cli/src/surface/detect.ts) and [packages/cli/src/surface/init.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/cli/src/surface/init.ts): framework, root, and package-manager detection; the diff and the install forms; [packages/cli/src/surface/api.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/cli/src/surface/api.ts) lists every SDK name the generated code uses.
- [docs/examples/auto/provider.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/auto/provider.ts), [docs/examples/auto/config.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/auto/config.ts), [docs/examples/auto/handler.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/auto/handler.ts), [docs/examples/auto/serve.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/auto/serve.ts): the provider, a config, a rule's handler, the generic tools.
- [docs/examples/host/page.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/host/page.ts), [docs/examples/host/dev.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/host/dev.ts), [docs/examples/host/production.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/host/production.ts): the page side of unattended mode, a development host, a production host with `sessionFor`.
- [docs/examples/relay/page.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/relay/page.ts), [docs/examples/relay/backend.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/relay/backend.ts), [docs/examples/relay/server.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/relay/server.ts): the attended fallback: connecting a tab, minting its token, a production relay.

## Decide your shape

Start with easy mode and go deeper only where a control needs it. Easy mode is the default for any web application; the deeper tiers are declared registration for controls whose truth the page cannot show, and server-side actions for operations with no control and for writes several people or agents share. Most applications end with a derived surface, a few declared entries, and some server actions. Pick the deeper tier by where the truth of "can this be done right now" lives, and by where the code that changes state runs. Before deciding, run the two local demos: `pnpm demo` (one file, [docs/examples/demo/plan-board.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/demo/plan-board.ts): a person and an agent on one plan, one revision, a conflict, a handoff; quick) and `pnpm example:dev` (the Next.js reference application: sessions, two tenants, conditional writes, approvals, browser-local controls).

- How the agent reaches it, the first decision: `axe surface init` includes the provider-injected path by default. Mount one provider above authentication and account/workspace resolution, and wire the structured profile to the application's existing auth source: `unknown` while resolving, `signed-out` on login, `signed-in` afterward. The provider-operated host runs the site in a private browser with no pairing. When it is signed out, the provider—not the application—offers a short-lived, revision-bound semantic form built from that session's standard visible sign-in fields; credentials never pass through chat or Surface, and the original request resumes only after Surface reports `signed-in`. Sensitive fields stay read-only to agents. Federated identity-provider redirects use a provider OAuth connector or brokered session rather than collecting those credentials in the generic form. Use `--relay-dev` only for the local code-pairing diagnostic. A browser agent can additionally use WebMCP directly when its host delivers page tools. Every route transports the page-owned surface rather than replacing it.
- Easy mode, the default: `SurfaceProvider` from `@summationai/axe-surface/react` near the root (what `axe surface init` writes), or `autoSurface({ root, config, expose })` from `@summationai/axe-surface/auto` on a page without React. The page's accessibility semantics are the source, so a control with a good accessible name and a real `disabled` state (with `aria-describedby` for its reason) needs nothing else; a `SurfaceConfig` rule fixes what the page cannot say (a name that states the outcome, the application's reason, a risk, `sensitive`, `hide`, `approval`, a `group`), and coverage lists what is left. Improving the page's markup improves the surface and the page's accessibility at once. Easy mode gives within-tab staleness, not a server-checked write: move a control to the declared tier (a rule's `handler`, or the hooks below) when its write must carry `expectedRev` to the server or when its truth lives off the page.
- Declared, in React (the deeper tier): the hooks and the derived scan share the module-level surface; coverage reports a derived entry that likely duplicates a declared one, and a rule with `hide: true` removes it. Where a component owns a control exactly, call `useSurface(entry, deps)` or `useSurfaceProps(entry, deps)` from `@summationai/axe-surface/react` once per control, inside the component that already computes the control's disabled state. `deps` names every value the entry reports (availability, reason, name, value), including transient flags (saving, loading, a modal open); left out, the surface keeps reporting a control available while the UI has frozen it ([S-REV-5]). Functions do not belong in `deps`: an act always runs the latest committed render's `handler`, `edit.set`, `more`, and `requires.fulfill`, and a new closure alone does not re-register. The registration belongs to the pair of the entry's `id` and the target surface: changing either unregisters the old pair and registers the new one (at the end of the table), unmount removes it, a refresh with the same id replaces the row in place, and Strict Mode's extra mount leaves the same table ([S-ENT-5]). Give each mounted control its own id; two components registering one id share a row and the first to unmount removes it. Rows rendered from a `.map` get a component that renders nothing and holds the hooks, so a row that leaves the page leaves the table. Spread `useSurfaceProps` onto the element that receives the interaction so the accessible name is the entry name ([S-DOM-1]); it reads the surface through `subscribe`, so a freeze or a registration made outside the component re-renders the control.
- `subscribe` versus `onChange` ([S-OBS-4]): `surface.subscribe(fn)` fires after every change a reader could see (`register`, a removing `unregister` or `reconcile`, `bump`, `setRev`, an adopting `seedRev`, `freeze`, `thaw`, `reset`), so a mirror outside React that re-applies `attributesFor` subscribes to it, especially under an application-owned revision. `onChange` fires on `bump`, `freeze`, and `thaw` only, never on registration, so a consumer that rebuilds per change of the action set is not woken once per row.
- Legacy or non-React DOM (HTML from string builders, `innerHTML`, jQuery, Web Components): write one pure re-scan adapter plus a thin sync in the renderer. After each render, the sync reads the application's own facts (data attributes, `disabled`, `readOnly`, lock records, app flags: the same state the renderer used to disable the control, never pixels or ARIA) into plain descriptors and hands them to a module with no DOM access and no framework or legacy imports, which calls `register` per control, `reconcile(prefix, keep)` per id prefix so rows that left the render leave the table, `setRev(appRevision)` or `bump()`, and `setObjects(() => domainObjects)`. One function holds every reason sentence and returns the application's words or null; the freeze reason shares its constant so the two paths cannot disagree. The field setter and the action handler run the exact commit the change event or the button runs. Because the module takes descriptors in and callbacks out, Node tests prove the reasons, the revision, and the freeze without a browser. Choose ids that carry the application's own keys (`cell:<metric>:<period>:<grain>`, `lock:<month>`); the per-control bridge slugs them for action names (`cell:a_b:2026-01:month` becomes `cell-a-b-2026-01-month`).
- Find every off-render state channel before writing the adapter: grep for how the application disables controls without re-rendering (a busy sweep, a mutation store, a storage gate, a protected-save lock). Each one needs a `freeze` or a re-sync subscribed to that channel; the render path alone misses exactly the state that caused the first trial's defect.
- Server-side operations with no UI control (the other deeper tier): write `action()`s by hand ([docs/designing-actions.md](docs/designing-actions.html)), or derive them with `@summationai/axe-generate` from an OpenAPI 3.x document (`fromOpenAPI`), a table of zod-typed functions (`fromFunctions`), or a tRPC router (`fromTRPCRouter`), then `generate` and `registerGenerated`. The generator leaves out any operation without a description or a risk for a mutation and says so in a warning; it never invents them. A consequential server action that needs a person's approval is a hand-written action with `approvalState` (see the consent rule below).
- Execution modes ([S-MODE-1] to [S-MODE-4]): a surface lives in the JavaScript realm that created it. Browser-local: a surface created in the page, with entries registered by its components, belongs to that tab and page instance; its handlers close over the page's state and act with the page's session, and only code in that page reaches it (`expose(window)`, `exposeWebMcp`, an in-page adapter, or `connectRelay`, which carries it to an outside agent while every act still runs in the page). Server-side: a surface created in a server process, or hand-written `action()`s, lives as long as the process and is served over AXE, scoped by the runtime to the caller's principal and tenant; it must never depend on a closure a browser registered. Importing the same module in a Next route handler creates a second, empty surface. The SDK's one broker is `@summationai/axe-relay` ([S-MODE-3], §9.1): a page that calls `connectRelay` is served to agents authenticated as the same person, with every act run in the page; nothing else carries entries, acts, observations, or sessions between a page and a server, between tabs, or between processes. State several people or agents share lives on the server behind server-side capabilities that write conditionally, and a page surface in `app` revision mode adopts the server's revision with `setRev`, so an agent in the page and an agent on the server present the same `expectedRev`. Unmount or navigation unregisters browser-local entries and changes nothing on the server. The runnable reference is `examples/plan-review`: plan reads, edits, submit, approve-and-lock, and history as server actions over AXE; cell drafts, Save, scrolling, and the approval dialog on a page surface at `window.__surface`; a table of who owns each capability in [docs/reference-app.md](docs/reference-app.html).
- Serving a surface as AXE actions: `createAXE({ ..., auth: { modes: ["user"], authenticate }, revision: surface.currentRev })`, then `axe.addProvider(surfaceActions(surface, { namespace }))`, then mount with `axeExpress`, `axeNext` or `axeNextPages`, `axeFetch`, or `axe.fetchHandler()`. The surface's revision becomes the site's: every envelope carries `rev`, a stale `expectedRev` is `conflict` before any handler runs, and `/axe/state` answers per control. With a resolver (below) leave `revision` off, or give a provider that resolves the caller itself, since the protocol's revision provider does not see the caller ([S-AUTH-4]).
- Who may observe and act over HTTP ([S-AUTH-1] to [S-AUTH-6], [S-PRV-1] to [S-PRV-3]): every action the bridge generates declares `auth`, default `"user"`, so a server whose `auth.modes` lacks `user` (including `createAXE`'s public default `{ modes: ["none"] }`) refuses the bridge on its first request instead of serving it. A public surface needs `auth: "none"` written by the integrator; the planning grid's in-process harness does exactly that (`surfaceActions(surface, { namespace: "grid", auth: "none" })` with `auth: { modes: ["none"] }`). `read` sets the mode of `<ns>.observe` and `<ns>.ledger` (default: `auth`), and `authFor(entry)` one entry's mode. A server hosting many users passes a resolver `(context) => Surface | null` with a `template` surface that fixes the action set; `scopedSurfaces({ create, key, max, idleMs, onEvict })` builds one keyed by tenant and principal, evicting beyond `max` (1000) and after `idleMs` (30 minutes). The manifest and anonymous `/axe/state` never read a protected surface; with a single protected surface, entry names are still public in the manifest, so private names need the resolver form. A field entry with `sensitive: true` carries no `value` in `observe()` (locally, through `expose`, and over HTTP), `describeEntry` says `value hidden`, WebMCP never offers it, and the ledger never keeps its text. `createSurface({ ledger: { text: "keep" | "hash" | "omit", redact } })` sets what the ledger keeps of other typed text (default `keep`; `hash` stores `textHash`, which links equal texts and does not hide guessable ones). `redactEvent` rewrites `surface.act` event details. `setObjects` is the application's; keep private data out of it or protect the read side.
- Granularity ([S-AXE-10] to [S-AXE-13], [S-OBS-5]): `surfaceActions` publishes one action per control; `domainActions` publishes `<ns>.observe`, `<ns>.ledger`, and a fixed set of parameterized actions (default `set-field`, `run-control` declared `risk: "high"`, `load-more`, or your own `DomainActionSpec`s with `covers(entry)`, `risk`, `idempotent`, `reversible`, `humanHandoff`, `idleReason`), each taking `{ entryId, text?, confirm? }` and running `surface.act` with the entry's own op, so the revision, ladder, ledger, and events are identical. An entry whose metadata exceeds its spec's, or whose text fails the honesty lint, is left uncovered and reported through `onError`. In both modes `<ns>.observe` filters and pages (`object`, `kind`, `available`, `query`, `limit`, `cursor`; output adds `total` and `nextCursor`; 1000 rows per page per control, 50 and at most 200 per domain action). Measured on a scripted demand plan ([docs/review/2026-09-24/data/granularity.md](docs/review/2026-09-24/data/granularity.html); payload sizes, not model behavior): the MCP `tools/list` is 72 KB per control against 11 KB for domain actions at 50 controls and 1325 KB against 11 KB at 1000, and over 50 UI changes per-control mode sent 18 to 21 `tools/list_changed` notifications against none. Use per control for small surfaces (tens of controls), UI parity, and tool lists a person reads; domain actions for large or churning surfaces and constrained contexts. Migrate side by side under two namespaces, then drop the per-control provider.
- Where the surface comes from: `createSurface({ app })` for an instance, or the module-level `surface` and its bound functions (`configure`, `register`, `unregister`, `reconcile`, `freeze`, `seedRev`, `setRev`, `currentRev`, `bump`, `onChange`, `setObjects`, `observe`, `act`, `ledger`, `record`, `expose`) exported from `@summationai/axe-surface`; `subscribe` and the other methods are on the object. `useSurface` and `useSurfaceProps` take an optional third argument naming the instance; the default is the module-level one, which the built `/react` entry now shares with `@summationai/axe-surface` (it used to carry a second registry). Passing the surface explicitly, as the reference app does, is clearest.
- Who owns the revision ([S-REV-1]): the surface has one revision mode at a time, `surface` or `app`, read with `surface.revisionMode()`. In `surface` mode the application's state lives in the browser and it calls `bump()` after every change an agent could observe, whoever made it, and `freeze` and `thaw` bump too. In `app` mode the application has a revision of its own (a server counter), adopts it with `setRev()` on every sync, keeps its own stale check as the second gate in the write itself ([S-ACT-11]), and `freeze` and `thaw` leave the revision alone, so an act planned before a freeze is `unavailable` while frozen and accepted afterwards exactly when the application's revision did not move ([S-FRZ-2], [S-FRZ-3]). The mode follows the last of `bump()` and `setRev()`, or is pinned with `createSurface({ revision: "surface" | "app" })`. When a handler learns the new revision itself (a protected mutation acknowledged by the server), return a `HandlerReport` `{ changed?, rev? }` from the handler, `edit.set`, or `more`: `act` adopts the `rev` as `setRev` would and reports the `changed` ids ([S-ACT-1], [S-LED-5]). A handler that returns nothing leaves `changed` empty in `app` mode, and agents re-observe. Never derive a revision from a content hash.
- [docs/auto-surface.md](docs/auto-surface.html): easy mode, the default tier, and how a rule's `handler` moves one control to the declared tier.
- [docs/surface.md](docs/surface.html): the guide to Surface, from registration to serving it; "Writing under a precondition", "Choosing granularity", "Who can observe and act", "Using it from React", and "Where a surface runs" are the sections an integrator needs.
- [spec/SURFACE.md](docs/spec/SURFACE.html): the normative contract (v0.9): terms, the three rules, entries, availability, observe and act, the ledger, freezes, the seam and its authorization, browser agents, WebMCP, execution modes.
- [docs/reference-app.md](docs/reference-app.html): Plan Review, how to run it, the ownership table, a code tour, and its deliberate limits.
- [examples/plan-review](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/examples/plan-review): the reference application's source; `lib/axe.ts` (server capabilities), `lib/browser-surface.ts` (the page surface), `lib/domain.ts` (one implementation of every change and its reasons).
- [packages/surface/src/react.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/surface/src/react.ts): `useSurface`, `useSurfaceProps`, `toSurfaceProps`.
- [packages/surface/src/axe.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/surface/src/axe.ts): `surfaceActions`, `domainActions`, `scopedSurfaces`, their options, the name map, the ladder mapping.
- [docs/examples/surface/access.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/surface/access.ts): protected and scoped surfaces, sensitive fields, the ledger text policy.
- [docs/examples/surface/granularity.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/surface/granularity.ts): domain actions, the side-by-side migration, and an agent's filtered observe and act.
- [packages/surface/test/fixtures/board.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/surface/test/fixtures/board.ts): the draft-board fixture that mirrors a real React row registration.
- [docs/examples/surface/serve.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/surface/serve.ts): the code that serves a surface as a manifest, and the name map in both directions.
- [docs/examples/surface/save.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/surface/save.ts): `freeze` around a save in flight.
- [docs/generating.md](docs/generating.html): deriving actions from OpenAPI, functions, or tRPC; overrides and policy; what the generator refuses to invent.
- [docs/live-state.md](docs/live-state.html): revisions, `expectedRev`, `availability`, `/axe/state`, the two gates, and how Surface plugs into them.

## Rules that are scars

Each rule below was paid for on a real application, found by the end-to-end trial of easy mode with the relay (the CHANGELOG's four-step section), or found by the 2026-09-24 engineering review, whose eighteen items each record the finding, the change, the tests that pin it, and the limits that remain ([docs/review/2026-09-24/README.md](docs/review/2026-09-24/README.html)). The rule ids are in [spec/SURFACE.md](docs/spec/SURFACE.html) and [spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.md](docs/spec/AXE-PROTOCOL.html).

- A derived surface moves the revision only for actionable changes, the trial's stale-act scar ([S-AUTO-6]): a control that appears, disappears, or changes its name, availability, or value moves it; a table's rows, a polled list, or live text do not, so a page that updates live does not refuse every act as `conflict`. Rows that carry controls still move it, because those controls are entries. Do not add a `bump()` for content changes on a derived page.
- Keep agents off the controls that govern agents, the trial's security fix: an auto-derived surface once read the relay's in-page indicator, so Stop, Approve, and Deny were controls an agent could see. Now the scan never reads a subtree marked `data-surface-ignore` (`IGNORE_ATTRIBUTE`), and always skips the relay's indicator whether marked or not, so an agent can never press the person's Stop, Approve, or Deny. Mark your own agent UI (a chat panel, an assistant drawer, a debug panel, your own relay indicator rendered from `onStatus`) `data-surface-ignore`, or exclude it with a config `exclude` selector.
- The person approves; the agent cannot ([S-AUTO-7], [S-AUTO-8], [S-RELAY-9]). Derived risk errs high: destructive words anywhere in the name, destructive styling, a control that opens an `alertdialog`, the affirmative button of a confirmation dialog, and every control the heuristics do not recognize are `high`, and the default policy is `approve` for `high`, so they wait for the person: the entry is unavailable with "needs the person's approval (...)" and a handoff with reason `approval_required` and no `url`. With the relay, the tab shows the request and approving it in the relay's panel also grants the derived gate (one decision, not two); granting or expiring an approval does not move the revision, so the agent's retry at the same `expectedRev` runs once. Denial is `forbidden` with `approval_denied`. Without the relay, `handle.approve(id, { uses, ttlMs })` records the approval, and it must be wired only to the person's own interaction in the page, never to anything an agent can reach (a tool, an exposed global, a control on the surface, a config `handler`). Lowering a risk in config is a reviewed statement that the control is safe for an agent; coverage lists every high-risk entry for that review.
- SSR-safe by construction ([S-AUTO-12]): nothing in `@summationai/axe-surface`, `@summationai/axe-surface/auto`, `@summationai/axe-surface/react`, or `@summationai/axe-relay/client` touches `window`, `document`, or `WebSocket` at import. Start everything in an effect: `SurfaceProvider` scans on mount, and `onReady(handle)` is where `connectRelay(handle.surface, ...)` goes (a static import is safe; a dynamic `import("@summationai/axe-relay/client")` there also keeps it out of the server bundle), returning `() => connection.disconnect()` as its cleanup. `stop()` is explicit user revocation, never component cleanup. Never call `autoSurface` or `connectRelay` at module scope.
- A tenant switch without a reload calls `connection.rekey()` ([S-RELAY-4]): the client leaves under the old identity, the relay drops the tab record and revokes its token, and it connects with a fresh `getToken()` for the new identity, so no agent of the old tenant reaches the page afterwards.
- Sensitive fields never cross the relay ([S-RELAY-8], [S-AUTO-9], [S-PRV-1]): the page sends what `observe()` and `ledger()` return, so a password, card field, one-time code, anything matching a config `sensitive` selector, or a rule's `sensitive: true` carries no value in any frame, observation, ledger, or coverage report, and is read only to agents unless a rule sets `editable: true`. The application's `objects`, the tab's title, and its path (never its query) do cross; keep private data out of them.
- Report, never decide ([S-RULE-1]): an entry's `state` and `reason` are whatever the application computed to enable or disable its own control. The adapter adds no authorization, validation, or business logic. Through AXE, `availability` is a report, not a gate: the handler is still the one door, and an unavailable action must not return `ok` ([P-LIVE-6]); `unavailable()` in `@summationai/axe-core` is the honest refusal with the same `reason`, `requires`, and `handoff` in `error.details`. The bridge's `auth` decides which callers reach the surface at all; it never writes an authorization message into a `reason` ([S-AUTH-3]).
- Same door ([S-RULE-2]): the handler an agent triggers is the handler a click or a change event runs, so authorization, validation, and persistence stay where they are. A Surface adapter that calls a service directly instead of the control's commit has opened a second path to state.
- One revision ([S-RULE-3]): every observation and every entry carries `rev`; every act presents `expectedRev`; a stale act is `error` `conflict` with `details: { expectedRev, currentRev }` and applies nothing ([S-ACT-2], [P-LIVE-3]). Through AXE the revision travels only as the request envelope's `expectedRev`, never in `input`; the per-row affordances that `<ns>.observe` returns carry it for the agent ([S-AXE-4]). A retried act with the same `expectedRev` after a success is refused, so a lost response cannot double-apply ([S-REV-2]).
- A preflight comparison is not concurrency control, the review's first Surface finding: two asynchronous acts presenting the same revision both ran and both returned `ok`. Now the acts on one surface run one at a time, every pre-handler check runs at the call, and an act that waited is checked again when it reaches execution, so a predecessor's commit, a person's `bump` or `setRev`, or a freeze makes it `conflict` or `unavailable` with no handler run ([S-ACT-9]). Under an app-owned revision a commit that reports nothing closes the claims queued behind it at that revision; reporting `changed: []` or `rev` avoids that ([S-ACT-10]). The queue orders one surface in one realm; two tabs or two clients are ordered only by the write itself. So a server-state handler takes the last argument, `ActContext` `{ id, op, expectedRev, actor }` (`handler(actor, text, context)`, `set(text, actor, context)`, `more(context)`), carries `context.expectedRev` into its conditional write (`UPDATE ... WHERE revision = $expectedRev`), and on a stale write refuses by throwing `new SurfaceConflict(message, { currentRev })` or returning `{ conflict: { currentRev } }`, having written nothing ([S-ACT-11]); on success it reports `{ changed, rev }`. A reported `rev` lower than the surface's by the time the handler settles is ignored and ledgered as `ignoredRev` ([S-REV-6]). In the planning grid this means the lock and unlock callbacks pass `context.expectedRev` as the protected protocol's expected revision and throw `SurfaceConflict` with the server's branch revision on refusal, and the cell commit reports `{ changed: [id], rev }` once the save lands, or an agent's second edit from one observation is `conflict` until it re-observes. A handler must never await `act` on its own surface; it would wait for itself.
- Bad targets, the first staging defect: an act whose `target` was `null` matched a row that was not actionable. Now `target` must be a non-empty string id or a non-negative integer index, and anything else is `invalid_input` at `/target` before any lookup ([S-ACT-6]); an index resolves only to the row whose `index` in the observation at that revision is that number, and a row without an index is unreachable by number ([S-ACT-7]); the revision guard runs before the target is resolved, so an index observed at an older revision is `conflict`, never the row that slid into its slot; an id that names an unavailable entry is `unavailable` with its reason, not `not_found` ([S-ACT-8]). Prefer ids ([S-ACT-5]).
- Frozen tables, the second staging defect: the table kept reporting cells editable while the application had disabled editing during a save, so an act ran into the frozen UI. Now the application must re-register or `reconcile` on every transient state ([S-REV-5]), and `freeze(reason)` makes the page-wide case one call: every entry reports unavailable with that reason, `observe()` carries `frozen: { reason }`, no row carries an `index`, an act is `unavailable` with `retryable: true`, the revision moves on `freeze` and again on `thaw` in `surface` mode and stays the application's in `app` mode, `registryVersion()` moves in neither, and freezes nest and are counted ([S-FRZ-1] to [S-FRZ-4]). The shape is `const thaw = surface.freeze("saving"); try { await persist(); } finally { thaw(); }`.
- Replace in place ([S-ENT-5]): re-registering an entry by id keeps its position. Unregister-then-register on refresh moves the row to the end and an agent's index with it.
- Consent is not an input flag: an agent passing `confirm: true` (Surface's `effect.confirm`, or any boolean in `input`) is the agent's own assertion. A consequential call returns `requestApproval({ url, instructions, whatAgentShouldSayToUser, preview })` from its handler, and the action declares `approvalState` (the state the approval is bound to, compared at the request, at the approval, and at the resume) and `onResume` ([P-APPR-1] to [P-APPR-9]). The result is `needs_human` with reason `approval_required`, expiring in one hour by default. Only the site's own page, from the person's session-authenticated and CSRF-protected request after its role check, calls `axe.approveHandoff(id, { approver, tenant })`; `axe.getHandoff(id, { tenant })` gives the page the recorded input, preview, state, and requester to show. A resume before approval is a retryable `conflict` (`handoffStatus: "open"`); a change to the bound state voids the request for good (`invalidated`); `axe.cancelHandoff(id, { by, tenant, reason })` cancels any unused handoff (`cancelled`); after approval `onResume` receives the approved input once and a repeat replays the receipt. Receipts and the approval events (`approval.requested`, `approval.approved`, `approval.cancelled`, `approval.invalidated`, `approval.executed`) carry no input, state, or preview. Offer undo only where it exists: the reference app declares `reversible: true` on its approve-and-lock because Reopen exists, and a freeze is the takeover that cancels open and approved requests.
- Retries replay; tokens are bound. Every continue, resume, and poll must present the same tenant and the same principal (user, site key, or both) that started it, re-verified on each follow-up; every refusal is the same `not_found` an unknown token gets, and nothing runs ([P-TOK-6], [P-TOK-7]). A workflow started with a site key continues with that key; a key verified without an `id` is scoped by a keyed hash of the key. A repeated continue (same kind and payload) or resume returns the original envelope ([P-REQ-9], [P-HAND-6]). One `idempotencyKey` sent twice at once runs once: the second gets a retryable `conflict` with `details.operationStatus: "in_progress"` and `Retry-After`, then the stored envelope; the same key with different input is a non-retryable `conflict`; an `error` result releases the claim, so a retry runs again ([P-OP-1] to [P-OP-4]). Handlers get `operationId`, stable across retries and instances: write it under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the change, or pass it to a payment provider as its idempotency key. The SDK promises one run at a time and a replayed result, not exactly-once effects: a crash between your commit and the stored result, or a handler that outlives `operationLeaseSeconds` (default 60), runs again. A token minted anonymously is a bearer credential; put `user` or `site` auth on actions whose follow-ups carry private data.
- Poll results require the action's auth: a terminal poll result is returned only after the poll token's tenant and principal are authorized, the same as for continue and resume, and concurrent polls run `onPoll` once ([P-POLL-1], [P-POLL-2]). A custom `pollUrl` you return from `pending({ pollUrl })` is your own endpoint, and the SDK does not authorize it.
- Browsers send cookies on a page's behalf. A `POST` to a non-`readOnly` action, `/axe/continue`, or `/axe/resume` must be `application/json` (or `+json`), else `unsupported` with `details.reason: "json_required"`; a `POST` carrying a `Cookie` from an `Origin` that is neither `baseUrl`'s nor trusted is `forbidden` with `cross_origin_refused`, before any body, identity, or token is read ([P-TRANS-1] to [P-TRANS-4]). Configure it with `createAXE({ requestPolicy: { trustedOrigins, originCheck, requireJsonContentType } })`; list every hostname that loads your pages in `trustedOrigins`, keep the session cookie `SameSite=Lax` or stricter, and use `originCheck: "always"` if you authenticate with HTTP auth or client certificates, which the runtime cannot see. Your own UI endpoints need the same policy; the reference app checks them with `isAcceptedOrigin` and `isJsonContentType` from `@summationai/axe-core`.
- The client sends credentials only where you said. `@summationai/axe-client` sends `auth` and `headers` only to the origin discovery started from plus `trust.origins`; a manifest `baseUrl`, `live.url`, `pollUrl`, or discovery hint on another origin is refused (`AXETrustError`, before anything is sent), or contacted without credentials under `trust.allowCrossOrigin`, which still refuses loopback and private-range names. Redirects are followed by hand and re-checked per hop, credentials never cross an origin, https-to-http is refused, and plain http is allowed only for loopback by default (`trust.allowHttp`). `trust.destinationPolicy` sees every outbound URL and `checkDestination(url)` answers without sending ([P-AGENT-4] to [P-AGENT-9]). The checks see names, not addresses: a host-side client (an agent running on your servers) also needs an egress policy, a proxy or firewall refusing private ranges and metadata endpoints, or an injected `fetch` that checks the resolved address. `@summationai/axe-mcp`'s `axe_poll` polls only a `pollUrl` the server itself returned.
- Limits are part of the contract ([P-LIM-1] to [P-LIM-4], [P-SCHEMA-1] to [P-SCHEMA-6]). `maxBodyBytes` defaults to 1 MiB: a larger body is refused with 413, `invalid_input`, `details.reason: "payload_too_large"`, before it is read; bodies nested deeper than 64 levels are `invalid_input`. Raise the limit only for inline `document.base64`. The client bounds each request with `timeoutMs` (30 s), `maxResponseBytes` (4 MiB), and polling with `maxPollAttempts` (60) and `maxWaitMs` (60 s, shared across a `run()`), and never polls faster than once a second. The validator implements a published JSON Schema subset ([docs/schemas.md](docs/schemas.html)) and refuses values under keywords, formats, or patterns it cannot apply instead of ignoring them; `schemaProblems` and the lint rules `unsupported-schema`, `backtracking-pattern`, and `refined-schema` find them first. A Zod refinement, custom type, or preprocess the manifest cannot express is marked `"x-axe-refined": true` in the published input schema. Idempotency fingerprints and token bindings hash `input` as sent, before defaults and transforms, so a filled-in default is a different request.
- Reasons are the application's own words: `reason` is plain language a person would recognize from the UI ("this version is locked", "already drafted by another team"), never a code and never an instruction to the agent. `requires` names AXE kinds the application can `fulfill`; `handoff` names a step a human can take, with a `url` only when a page to come back from exists ([S-AV-3]). A handoff without a `url` is reported in `error.details.handoff` by `act` and stays `error` `unavailable` through the bridge; only a handoff with a `url` becomes `needs_human` ([S-AXE-2]). Never invent a URL, a kind, a description, or a risk; when a definition does not say, leave the action out (the generator's rule) or ask the owner.
- Names state the outcome, not the widget ([S-DOM-1]): "Lock March", not "Lock button"; the role is `role`, the state is `state`. The same string is the control's `aria-label` and the `name` in `observe()`. A name that reads like an instruction ("click here to lock") fails the honesty lint and the bridge drops the entry (`onError` warns once), so write outcomes.
- The DOM mirror is applied from the renderer, on the same channels that change availability: `surface.attributesFor(id)` returns `{ set, remove }` from the entry's live availability, freeze included, where `remove` is every canonical attribute (`SURFACE_ATTRIBUTES`) not in `set`; apply both on the element that receives the interaction, so a cell that became editable again does not keep last render's reason, and never overwrite an `aria-label` the application already renders. `surfaceAttributes(entry)` is the one-time form for a render that has the entry in hand; `useSurfaceProps` follows live availability on its own ([S-DOM-1]).
- What the ledger records ([S-LED-1], [S-LED-8], [S-AXE-14], [S-RELAY-7]): every act through the surface, run or refused (through the relay under the actor `<principal> (agent via relay)`); every change the application recorded with `surface.record` (marked `source: "application"`); and, through the bridge, every refusal the runtime made before the handler for a caller it admitted (a stale `expectedRev`, an input that fails the schema, a missing `idempotencyKey`; marked `source: "server"`, recorded once, no new action event). Nothing else: a call refused for an unadmitted caller, or before the server knew the caller or the action, is only in the request events. A ledger entry's `source` (`application` or `server`; absent for an act) says who wrote the entry and is not an observe row's `tier`, which says how the entry was made. The surface's own input checks (`maxLength`, a field's schema, a required `confirm`) run in the surface and are ledgered as `invalid_input`; the bridge's action input schemas describe the shape only.
- A change made outside `act` leaves a revision gap unless it is recorded, the scar from demoing the Plan Board over MCP: "Approve March" moved the revision with no entry, and the agent's stale February edit, refused at the server's gate, was missing from a ledger whose description said every refusal was in it. Now the demo records the approval with `surface.record({ op, target, actor, changed, revBefore })` (make the change and move the revision first; `record` runs no handler and moves nothing), and the bridge records the server's refusal through the provider `onResult` that `addProvider` wires.
- `act` is asynchronous. `window.__surface.act(...)` returns a promise; a browser agent that reads `.code` off the return value without awaiting it reads nothing.
- No agent-directed text and no persuasion ([P-HON-1], [P-HON-2]): every string an agent reads (`name`, `reason`, `instructions`, `whatAgentShouldSayToUser`, every `description`) is linted with `lintAgentText`; an entry whose text fails is reported through the bridge's `onError` and left out of the action set, and the audit zeroes its Trustworthy category on an agent-directed imperative.
- Effect metadata is truthful ([S-EFF-1], [S-EFF-2], [P-HON-7]): `risk` is never `none` for an action entry and defaults to `medium`; `reversible` is the name, `undoable` a deprecated alias; a control that changes state is never presented as read-only. A domain action's metadata must hold for every entry it covers ([S-AXE-11]).
- The ledger keeps refusals ([S-LED-4]): an agent that observed at one revision and was refused at another did nothing, and the record says so. The ledger is in memory and bounded (`ledger.max`, default 1000); the durable trail is the `surface.act` action events on the server's `onActionEvent` sinks ([S-AXE-5]), which carry no text or values.
- [spec/SURFACE.md](docs/spec/SURFACE.html): the rules by id, and the Provenance section that names the defects.
- [docs/examples/surface/precondition.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/surface/precondition.ts): a handler carrying `expectedRev` into a conditional write and refusing with `SurfaceConflict`.
- [docs/human-oversight.md](docs/human-oversight.html): the approval flow, the page's obligations, what is bound where, cancellation, receipts.
- [docs/examples/human-oversight/approval.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/human-oversight/approval.ts): an action with `approvalState` and the approval page's handler.
- [docs/auth.md](docs/auth.html): the three modes, site keys, and "Cookie sessions" (the request policy matrix and options).
- [docs/security.md](docs/security.html): the threat model, each mitigation with the review item whose tests pin it, what your site must provide, known gaps.
- [DECISIONS.md](docs/repo/DECISIONS.html): the Relay, Easy mode, Surface, Live state, Client trust, Limits and schema boundaries, and Human oversight and execution modes sections; "Two staging defects are rules, not fixes", "The idempotency store claims; it does not get and set", "The revision stays global; a per-entry precondition is a proposal, not code".
- [docs/audit.md](docs/audit.html): the honesty rules and what the audit rejects.

## Packaging

- Workspace: pnpm 10 (via corepack) and Turborepo, Node 22 or newer to develop (CI runs Node 22 and 24; jsdom needs 22; the published packages keep their declared range and are built for `node20`, but Node 20 is no longer tested), packages under `packages/*`, the reference app under `examples/*` (outside `pnpm -r build`, inside `pnpm -r test`). `pnpm install`, then `pnpm -r build`, `pnpm -r typecheck`, `pnpm -r test`, `pnpm lint`. Every package is built by tsup from `tsup.base.ts` (`platform: "neutral"`, `target: "node20"`) as ESM plus CJS with `exports` conditions and declares `sideEffects: false`.
- Subpaths: `@summationai/axe-core` exports `.`, `./types`, `./vocabulary`, `./kinds`, `./events`, `./display`, `./lint`, `./schemas`, `./json-schema` (`validateJsonSchema`, `schemaProblems`, `isBacktrackingPattern`, `SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_KEYWORDS`, `schemasStructurallyEqual`, `deepEqual`), and `./node`; `./types`, `./display`, `./vocabulary`, `./lint`, and `./json-schema` are zod-free, and `./node` (`jsonlFileSink`, `SqliteIdempotencyStore`) is the one entry that needs Node. `@summationai/axe-surface` exports `.`, `./react`, `./auto`, `./axe`, and `./webmcp`; `react` (18 or newer; 18 and 19 tested) is an optional peer dependency, so a server-only surface carries no React. `@summationai/axe-relay` exports `./client` and `./token` (browser-safe; neither imports anything at runtime), `./server`, and `./cli`, with the `axe-relay` bin; the `axe` CLI's `axe relay` runs the same code. The built `/react`, `/auto`, and `/webmcp` entries import the main entry instead of inlining it (and `SurfaceProvider` and `autoActions` import `./auto.js` at runtime), so the hooks, the derived scan, the WebMCP adapter, and `surface.expose(window)` share one registry (one per module format; an application that loads the main entry as ESM and `/react` as CommonJS still gets two).
- Durable stores: the in-memory `MemoryTokenStore` and `MemoryIdempotencyStore` are correct for one process, bounded (`maxEntries` 10000, swept on writes every `sweepIntervalMs`), and lose everything on restart. Production with more than one instance needs a shared `tokenStore` (get/set with TTLs is enough) and an `idempotencyStore` whose `claim` is atomic: `SqliteIdempotencyStore` from `@summationai/axe-core/node` over a `node:sqlite` connection you supply (one host; call `prune()` on a schedule), the Redis Lua scripts in [docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.html) ("Secrets and stores"; typechecked, not executed in CI, atomic on one primary), or your database's conditional insert. `createAXE` refuses an idempotency store with only `get` and `set`, because a read followed by a write lets two requests run. Migrating a custom store: implement `get`, `claim`, `complete`, and `release`; the record field is now `fingerprint`; `TokenRecord.onBehalfOf` is now `principal`; tokens minted before the upgrade return `not_found`, so deploy in a quiet period.
- Body parsers: mount `axeExpress` before `express.json()`. The runtime then reads the raw stream up to `maxBodyBytes` and answers an oversized body with an envelope; a parser in front applies its own limit (100 kB for `express.json()`) and answers with its own error page. Either way the adapters keep the `Content-Type` the client sent, so the request policy judges the real body.
- npm: releases go through changesets (`pnpm release` runs `pnpm build && changeset publish`, `access: public`, all packages version together as `@summationai/axe-*` and `axe`). Version 0.1.0 is unreleased at the time of writing; nothing in this repository shows a published `@axe` scope, so do not `npm install @summationai/axe-surface` and expect it to resolve.
- Vendored tarballs while unpublished: `scripts/pack-for-consumer.sh <out-dir> [package ...]` builds the workspace and packs the named package directories (default `core surface client testing`; the arguments replace the default, they do not add to it). A desktop-agent Surface app packs `scripts/pack-for-consumer.sh <out> core surface relay`; a WebMCP-only app can omit `relay`. Each lands in `<out-dir>` as `summationai-axe-<name>-<version>.tgz`, beside `<out-dir>/SOURCE` with the repository, branch, commit, and date. The tarball carries the version, not the commit, and 0.1.0 covers every pre-release commit, so that file is the pin; commit it beside the tarballs. pnpm rewrites `"@summationai/axe-core": "workspace:*"` to `"@summationai/axe-core": "0.1.0"` in the packed manifest, so the consumer declares each package as a `file:` dependency and points siblings back at their tarballs with its package-manager override; `axe surface init --vendor <dir>` writes the right one. `@summationai/axe-relay`'s server dependencies (`@summationai/axe-mcp`, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, `ws`) are optional peers, installed only in the provider-operated service. `npm ci` resolves `file:` tarballs with no registry and no auth, so a Dockerfile copies the vendor directory before the install; refresh and commit the lockfile with the tarballs.
- GitHub Packages: its npm registry serves only the scope that matches the GitHub owner, so a repository under `summationai` can publish `@summationai/*` there and not `@summationai/axe-*`; renaming the packages, npm, or tarballs are the options.
- Browser bundling: `@summationai/axe-surface` and the hook-only imports from `@summationai/axe-surface/react` carry no Zod, Node built-ins, derivation, or WebMCP code. `SurfaceProvider` carries the derived scan and its small WebMCP adapter because it can expose browser-native tools; tree shaking removes both when only hooks are imported. `@summationai/axe-surface/webmcp` also bundles alone without React or Zod. The desktop-agent integration adds only `@summationai/axe-relay/client`; its MCP SDK, WebSocket server, and Node dependencies remain in the provider-operated service. `@summationai/axe-surface/axe` carries Zod through `@summationai/axe-core`, so keep the bridge on the server. A Zod schema on a field entry needs `createSurface({ toJsonSchema })` with `toJsonSchema` from `@summationai/axe-core`, which brings Zod with it; a plain JSON Schema needs nothing. Measure your own bundle with `esbuild --metafile` before and after.
- [docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.html): "Secrets and stores", "Operations, claims, and crashes", "Migrating a store", "Limits and retention", and "Consume from a checkout".
- [docs/examples/deploying/stores.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/deploying/stores.ts): the Redis stores and the `operationId` pattern, as code.
- [docs/integrations/express.md](docs/integrations/express.html): middleware order and body parsing.
- [scripts/pack-for-consumer.sh](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/scripts/pack-for-consumer.sh): the packing script.
- [packages/surface/test/bundle.test.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/surface/test/bundle.test.ts) and [packages/relay/test/bundle.test.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/relay/test/bundle.test.ts): the browser-bundle pins.
- [packages/relay/package.json](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/relay/package.json): the relay's entries and its optional server peers.
- [package.json](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/package.json): scripts (`demo`, `example:dev`, `eval`, `measure:granularity`), `packageManager`, engines.
- [tsup.base.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/tsup.base.ts): the shared build options.
- [packages/surface/package.json](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/surface/package.json): exports, the optional React peer.
- [packages/surface/tsup.config.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/surface/tsup.config.ts): the shared-registry build plugin.
- [packages/core/package.json](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/packages/core/package.json): the subpath exports.
- [.changeset/config.json](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/.changeset/config.json): release configuration.
- [docs/api/README.md](docs/api/README.html): the package table and entry points.

## Reach it through existing agent interfaces

The same actions and surface reach agents through interfaces those agents already speak. Pick by where the agent runs.

- A consumer ChatGPT user, the target production integration: install the package under `plugins/agent-experience`, connect the provider account through OAuth, and use the provider's public hosted `mcp/` endpoint. The first relevant `relay_tabs` starts or resumes an isolated private browser; `@summationai/axe-host` injects a scoped relay before application code runs. A brokered `sessionFor` may start it already signed in. Without one, the root-mounted Surface reports `signed-out` and the provider offers a short-lived semantic form for that private session's standard first-party sign-in steps; the person signs in there without putting credentials in chat, then `axe_resume` replays the original request. The customer app adds no auth route, backend broker, remote-browser code, or MCP server. After authentication, organization/tenant state and all behavior still come from Surface.
- The same client driving the person's own live tab, attended, the fallback: the relay, `@summationai/axe-relay` ([docs/relay.md](docs/relay.html)). The page connects with `connectRelay(surface, { url, getToken, onStatus, indicator, requireApproval })`; the relay serves each tab through `domainActions` on a `createAXE` server and `@summationai/axe-mcp` derives the tools, over Streamable HTTP (sessions, OAuth `agentAuth`) or stdio. The indicator in the page shows that an agent is connected and offers Stop and the approvals; `indicator: false` means your UI renders them from `onStatus` and calls `connection.stop()`, `approve(id)`, and `deny(id)`. Stop revokes the token and refuses every later act on that tab with `forbidden`; a reload is not Stop, and an act sent during it waits for the new page. Revisions presented through the relay are the tab's plus an offset, so one read before a reload or from another tab never passes ([S-RELAY-6]).
- MCP over stdio: `axe mcp <url>` (or `serveStdio(await createMcpServer(source))`) serves one user, with the credential given on its command line (`axe mcp <url> --auth <token>`) or in `createMcpServer`'s `client` options.
- MCP over HTTP: `serveHttp(derived, options)` returns a fetch handler for the Streamable HTTP transport. Stateless by default (a fresh MCP server and transport per request, no server-to-client stream, no `tools/list_changed`), or `sessions: true | { idleTimeoutMs, maxSessions }` (one server per `Mcp-Session-Id`, bound to the principal that opened it, 404 after `DELETE` or 30 minutes idle, held in one process's memory, so behind a load balancer use session affinity or stateless mode). `auth: { verifier, requiredScopes, resource, resourceMetadataUrl, principal }` makes the endpoint an OAuth 2.1 resource server: it verifies the bearer token on every request and answers 401 or 403 with `WWW-Authenticate`; `protectedResourceMetadata` serves the RFC 9728 document. It does not issue tokens; your authorization server does. `clientFor(authInfo)` runs for every tool call and returns that caller's AXE identity (`identity` and `tenant` for an in-process `AXE` source, or `client` options with the caller's own credential for a URL source, for example from a token exchange); the MCP token is never passed through to the site. `serveHttp` refuses a `createMcpServer` given shared `client.auth` or `client.headers` without `clientFor`, unless `allowSharedCredentials: true` says the endpoint has one user. `allowedOrigins` guards against DNS rebinding ([P-MCP-1] to [P-MCP-3]).
- Freshness: a URL or manifest source never derives tools from a manifest older than `min(manifestMaxAgeMs, the site's max-age)` (default five minutes), revalidates with the manifest's `ETag`, refreshes once on an unknown tool name or a `not_found`, and tells sessions when the tool list changed; `derived.refresh()` and the client's `refresh()`, `ensureFresh()`, `isManifestStale()`, and `onManifestChange()` do it on demand ([P-DISC-13], [P-MCP-4]). There is no background refresh; a timer calling `refresh()` is the host's.
- Retries through MCP: every tool for a mutating action accepts an optional `idempotencyKey`. A host that retries an uncertain call with the same key and arguments gets the stored envelope, or `in_progress` while the first still runs; without a key each call is a new operation. `axe_continue` and `axe_resume` accept `expectedRev` when the manifest carries `live` ([P-MCP-5]).
- Elicitation ([P-MCP-6], [P-MCP-7]): with a client that declared `elicitation`, on a connection that can carry a server request (stdio, in-memory, HTTP sessions; not stateless HTTP), a `needs_input` whose first suitable kind is not sensitive and fits MCP's flat form subset is asked in a form and continued; a sensitive kind (`sensitive: true`, every `payment.*` and `identity.*`, credentials) and a `needs_human` other than `login_required` are offered as the site's page in URL mode when the client supports it, else returned as text. `elicitation: false` turns it off.
- MCP Apps view ([P-MCP-8]), experimental: for a host that negotiated `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`, tools for `display` actions carry a `ui://axe/presentation` view that renders the escaped `toHTML` output with scripts removed. `apps: false` turns it off. Tested under jsdom with a stand-in host, not in a shipping host.
- WebMCP, the browser's own agent ([S-WEB-1] to [S-WEB-5]): `<SurfaceProvider webMcp>` or `exposeWebMcp(surface, { prefix, actor, unavailable, observe, content, run, requestApproval })` registers `surface_observe`, `surface_read` and `surface_wait` when derived page content exists, and one tool per action, non-sensitive field, and loadable collection with `document.modelContext.registerTool`; it re-registers when a tool's text or schema changes and runs each permitted control call through `surface.act`. Consequential calls require the trusted application callback `requestApproval(request)`; absent or denied approval is returned as an error and never reaches the handler. The adapter records the person's decision and may grant the internal one-use auto-surface gate. WebMCP is a draft API, so the adapter is feature-detected, registers nothing where absent (`supported: false` with the reason), reports registration health through `diagnostic()`, and the fallback is `expose(window)` and the DOM mirror. That fallback is browser-local JavaScript/DOM, not a promise that a generic headless browser task receives Surface tools.
- Browser-driving agents: the DOM mirror (`aria-label`, `data-surface-*`, `aria-disabled` with `data-surface-reason`) and `window.__surface` after `expose(window)` (a derived surface adds `coverage()` there). Both are browser-local and add no reader the page did not have; neither reaches a server.
- AXE clients: `@summationai/axe-client` directly ([docs/for-agent-builders.md](docs/for-agent-builders.html)), under the credential rules in Rules that are scars.
- [docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.html): the mapping table, "HTTP: requests, sessions, and cleanup", "Authentication over HTTP", elicitation, the Apps view, freshness, retries, limits.
- [docs/examples/mcp/oauth.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/mcp/oauth.ts): a resource server with in-process identity and the metadata route.
- [docs/examples/mcp/remote.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/mcp/remote.ts): a URL source with a per-caller credential.
- [docs/examples/mcp/elicitation.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/mcp/elicitation.ts): what elicitation asks and when.
- [docs/webmcp.md](docs/webmcp.html): status of the draft, feature detection, what is and is never registered, the fallback.
- [docs/examples/webmcp/page.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/webmcp/page.ts): `expose` and `exposeWebMcp` on one page surface.
- [docs/examples/for-agent-builders/trust.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/for-agent-builders/trust.ts): the client's `trust` options.

## Ship behind a flag, staging first

- Grow the manifest one action at a time behind a flag: a read-only action always on, a mutating action registered only when its flag is on; flip the flag in one environment, run `axe conformance` there, then flip it everywhere ([docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.html), "Rolling out one action at a time"). Agents read the manifest and act on it, so an action that appears in production is in production.
- Easy mode is enabled by default: `axe surface init` wraps the root in a provider that derives browser-local controls in every environment, exposes diagnostics only in development, registers WebMCP only where the browser supports it, and connects outside the browser only when a trusted provider injects a scoped connection. Add `--flag`, a named check, or a flag hook only for a deliberate staged rollout; an injected provider connection remains enabled so authentication and account/workspace selection cannot deadlock behind an application flag.
- Gate a hand-written Surface adapter the same way: one runtime flag (the planning grid reads its runtime profile) checked at the top of the sync function and the mirror, so with the flag off nothing registers, no attribute is set, no provider is added, and the page is byte-identical to before. Have the same runtime profile report the Surface contract version (v0.9 at the time of writing; read it from the header of `spec/SURFACE.md` at the pinned commit), the SDK name, and the pinned SDK commit from the vendor pin file, so a deploy can be matched to an SDK commit when a trial finds something.
- Upgrading an integration made against an earlier contract: a public bridge now needs `auth: "none"` or fails its first request with an auth-mode error; posts to mutating actions need `Content-Type: application/json`; a custom idempotency store needs `claim`; clients that relied on a cross-origin `baseUrl`, `live.url`, or `pollUrl` list it in `trust.origins`; `serveHttp` with shared credentials needs `clientFor` or `allowSharedCredentials`; server-state handlers should adopt `ActContext` and `SurfaceConflict`. The CHANGELOG's review sections carry each migration note.
- `axe conformance` calls mutating actions: it replays for idempotency, continues a `needs_input` with a sample payload, resumes a fallback handoff, and streams an oversized body. Run it against staging or a local instance with a disposable database; `--no-mutate` for an environment you cannot reset; never production with credentials.
- Staging is where the seam shows its defects. Both staging defects above were found there, and the easy-mode trial's three (the indicator on the surface, a live table refusing acts, two approvals for one act) end to end, in the seam between Surface and the application, not in either alone. Watch the ledger and the `surface.act` events during the trial, then widen.
- Before production: `secret` from a secret manager (16 characters or more); shared stores with an atomic idempotency `claim` and scheduled cleanup (`prune()`, TTLs); `operationLeaseSeconds` above the slowest handler and `operationId` passed downstream; `maxBodyBytes` at the default unless an inline document needs more, with any proxy or parser in front allowing at least that; every page origin in `requestPolicy.trustedOrigins`; `axe audit --min-score` as a CI gate; and `deprecated: { since, replacedBy }` instead of removing an action.
- [docs/deploying.md](docs/deploying.html): secrets and stores, limits and retention, discovery, CORS, caching, rate limiting, observability hooks, rollout, the checklist.
- [docs/examples/deploying/flags.ts](https://github.com/summationai/agent-experience/blob/main/docs/examples/deploying/flags.ts): the flag gate and the deprecation, as code.
- [docs/testing-and-conformance.md](docs/testing-and-conformance.html): running conformance locally and in CI, every check and what it verifies.
- [CHANGELOG.md](docs/repo/CHANGELOG.html): the migration note for each review item.

## Tests to write

- Easy mode, in the application: run `axe surface coverage` before and after each config change and keep the reports (the gaps left, and why, are the review). Under jsdom, mount the provider and assert that the flag off renders exactly what it rendered before; that a destructive control is unavailable with `approval_required` until the person approves in the page; that an act with an old `expectedRev` is `conflict` with nothing applied; that a live table updating does not move the revision while a control appearing does; that your agent UI marked `data-surface-ignore` is not on the surface; and that no sensitive field reports a value. Run `checkConfig` over the config in a unit test and `lintAgentText` over every `name` and `reason` it sets. Assert on keys from coverage (or pinned ids), not on positions.
- Two layers are enough for a hand-written adapter, and neither needs a server or a browser. Layer one, pure adapter tests: feed plain descriptors to the adapter and assert on `observe()`. Reasons are the application's words; `index` is set only on rows that can be acted on; the application's revision is adopted as `rev`; a re-sync drops rows that left the render (`reconcile`) and moves the revision with the application; an act with a stale `expectedRev` is `conflict` and runs nothing; a fresh one runs the application's own commit with the text and the actor; an action's `effect` and its name say the outcome (a lock carries the reason text, an unlock does not); a save in flight freezes the whole table with the shared reason on both channels (the render path and the mutation channel) and thawing restores it; the ledger names the actor for every act and every refusal and `observe().ledgerSeq` is the latest; every id round-trips through `surfaceSelector`. Tests that live outside the package root cannot import the SDK by bare specifier unless the app installed it, so run them where `node_modules` resolves.
- Layer two, an in-process AXE proof: `createAXE({ name, description, baseUrl, revision: surface.currentRev })` with either `auth: { modes: ["user"], authenticate }` and the bridge's default, or the public default (`auth` omitted is `{ modes: ["none"] }`) and `surfaceActions(surface, { namespace, auth: "none" })`; then `axe.addProvider(...)` and `axe.handle(new Request(...))` with `Content-Type: application/json` for the manifest, `<ns>.observe`, one action with the observed `expectedRev` and a stale one, and `/axe/state` during a freeze; and `runConformance` pointed at a `fetch` that routes into `axe.handle` and serves a `/` page with `<link rel="axe-manifest">` plus a `/robots.txt`, so the discovery checks and the six `live.*` checks pass. With a protected bridge, assert that an anonymous request to observe, the ledger, and an entry action is refused and that the anonymous manifest and `/axe/state` carry no value or reason.
- Two gates: start two acts presenting the same `expectedRev` with a handler held on a promise the test resolves (no sleeps) and assert one `ok` and one `conflict` with nothing applied twice; with a fake store whose write applies only at the expected revision, assert that two surfaces (two tabs) at the same revision commit once and the loser's handler refused with `SurfaceConflict`.
- A bundle test, if the surface ships in a browser bundle: bundle the entry with esbuild for the browser in a test and assert the size and the absence of Node built-ins, the way `packages/surface/test/bundle.test.ts` does for the package itself.
- Two-actor conflict: observe at one revision, let the other participant change state (`bump` or `setRev`), act with the old revision, and assert `conflict` with `details.expectedRev` and `details.currentRev`, nothing applied, and a ledger entry with that status; re-observe and continue from the new state. Add the index-shift case (a row that slid into an observed slot is not hit) and the lost-response case (the same revision retried after a success applies at most once).
- Freeze: `freeze("saving")` makes every entry unavailable with that reason, `observe().frozen` is set, an act is `unavailable` and `retryable`, `thaw()` restores the entries and moves the revision again in `surface` mode; nested freezes report the newest reason and thaw on the last release.
- Bad targets: `null`, `""`, `-1`, `1.5`, an object, and a missing target are `invalid_input` at `/target`; a number no row carries is `not_found`; an id that names an unavailable entry is `unavailable` with its reason.
- React, mounted: render with `react-dom/client` under jsdom, not static markup, which never runs an effect; assert an id change moves the registration, an act runs the latest render's handler, and a freeze reaches the control's props.
- Approvals, if an action needs consent: a resume before approval runs nothing; an agent's `confirm` flag approves nothing; a state change after the request invalidates it; a cancel stops it; the approved resume runs once and a repeat replays the receipt.
- In-process AXE tests with `@summationai/axe-testing`: `createTestClient(axe, { identity })` and `invokeAction(axe, name, input)` run the same code path as `/axe/actions/{name}`, `/axe/continue`, and `/axe/resume` without a port. Then `runConformance(url)` against the running application; when the manifest carries `live`, the six `live.*` checks run: `live.state-endpoint`, `live.rev-on-envelopes`, `live.stale-conflict`, `live.fresh-accepted`, `live.reasons`, `live.availability-honored`; the runtime checks include `runtime.json-content-type`, `runtime.body-limit`, and `runtime.nesting-limit`, and `ladder.token-principal` runs with `--auth`. A skipped check was not verified: "Conformant" means no check failed. `runAudit` with a floor completes the gate; a skipped check earns nothing there.
